EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Assam had three waves of flood in the year 2025, causing substantial loss of lives and property and severely
impacting the economy of the State. Out of total 35 districts of Assam, 28 districts have been affected by
flood in this year affecting approximately 11.19 lakh people in 3,255 villages. The death toll due to floods
and landslides has been 36. Besides, substantial damages to standing crops, infrastructures like, roads,
bridges, irrigation facilities, health facilities, schools, Livestock population etc. has also been reported from
the affected districts and respective line departments.
The State Government has undertaken substantial rescue and relief operation in the State in all waves of
flood. Based on ground assessment carried out with the help of District Administrations and the
Departments of the State Government, this Flood Memorandum has been finalised.
As such, based on the damage reports received from the Districts and the Departments, fund requirement
is estimated to be Rs. 2871.21 crore which includes an amount of Rs 62.98 Cr. for rescue and relief operation,
Rs. 10.26 Cr. for sectoral damages other than Core Critical Infrastructure (like Fish seeds, Replacement of
Animals, Assistance to Small and Marginal Farmers and Assistance to Artisans), Rs. 28.23 for damages in
Housing Sector and Rs. 2769.74 Cr. for repairing and restoration of immediate nature for various
infrastructure damaged during the flood.
The State is in need of large-scale financial assistance to recover from the extensive damages and losses due
to floods. The fund allotted for the State under SDRF will not be sufficient to meet the expenditure.
Assistance from NDRF will immensely help the state to recover at the earliest.

Assam falls in the highest rainfall intensity zone of the country. The precipitation here is mainly due to
the South-West monsoon i.e. June to September. Average annual rainfall in the region is very high and
ranges from 1750 mm in the plains to about 6400 mm in the hills. High rainfall in the state & upper
catchment in the neighbouring states like Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Mizoram, Manipur
and neighbouring country (Bhutan) causes severe floods in Assam almost every year. This huge volume
of water rushes through the narrow bowl-shaped valley of Assam to the Bay of Bengal ravaging the area
through which it flows with floods and erosion.
Assam comprises of a large network of rivers and tributaries. These rivers and tributaries originate from
the Upper Catchments with high gradient and join Brahmaputra and the Barak river to form a highly
dynamic and complex river system.
The length of the Brahmaputra River is 2880 km. It has a catchment area of 5,80,000 Sq. km in Tibet,
Bhutan, China, India and Bangladesh and in terms of discharge, it is the third largest river in the world..
The River flows for a length of 640 Km through the plains of Assam (Tinsukia to Dhubri). In this valley,
about 64 tributaries on its North bank and about 38 on its South bank join the river Brahmaputra. The
total length of embankment in Assam is 2745 Km.
The river Barak is the second largest river in the North East, originating from Nagaland and Manipur, it
traverses a length of 225 Km in Assam and flows into Bangladesh. The total number of tributaries joining
the Barak river within its Assam reach is around 10 and the number of sub tributaries joining the main
tributaries is around 5. The catchment area of tributaries ranges between 300-4200 sq. km. and that of
the sub tributaries ranges between 100- 2000 sq. km. Total length of embankment in Assam is 526 Km.
The extreme monsoon regime vis-à-vis the unique physiographic setting of the basin has been
considered as the single most important cause for frequent occurrence of flood in this region. Besides,
deforestation in the upstream areas lying in Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Mizoram,
Manipur and Bhutan is resulting in excessive siltation and runoff, decreasing the carrying capacity of
major rivers and tributaries.
Assam has approximately 5,000 Km of embankments constructed on the recommendation of Rashtriya
Barh Aayog as short term measures in the decades of 1950s and 60s. The embankments have outlived
their lives.
(Source: Assam River Atlas- 2020)

2.1 Assam Floods in 2025:
This year , Assam has faced three waves of floods till date, which have affected 28 districts of the state,
resulting in loss of human lives, livestock and large scale damage to the dwelling houses, standing crops,
infrastructure like roads, bridges, embankments, schools, AWCs etc.
Notified Flood season starts in Assam from 1st May till 31st October every year and during the period
ASDMA generates daily flood situation reports digitally through DRIMS (Disaster Reporting and
Information Management System). Each Revenue Circle of Assam submits an online situation report
through its respective DDMAs in the DRIMS portal. Following 28 districts of Assam have been affected
by floods this year viz. Barpeta, Biswanath, Bongaigaon, Cachar, Charaideo, Darrang, Dhemaji, Dibrugarh,
Dima-Hasao, Goalpara, Golaghat, Hailakandi, Hojai, Jorhat, Kamrup, Kamrup (M), Karbi Anglong,
Kokrajhar, Majuli, Morigaon, Nagaon, Sivasagar, Sonitpur, South Salmara, Sribhumi, Tinsukia, Lakhimpur
and West Karbi Anglong
Preparedness measures taken by ASDMA before floods:
As part of the flood preparedness initiatives, Assam State Disaster Management Authority (ASDMA) had
conducted six thematic meetings for flood preparedness during March- April 2025 with all line
departments, Central Agencies and stakeholders. These thematic meetings are viz. (i) Coordination for
Response with responding agencies, (ii) Critical Infrastructure Preparedness, (iii) Ensuring continuity
of services viz. Health, Water & Sanitation, Education, Social welfare services etc., (iv) Relief Camp
Management, (v) Risk communication and (vi) Reporting and Damage Assessment as part of its
preparedness this year with various stakeholders.
Besides, ASDMA also conducted multi layered review of Flood Preparedness, which includes- (i) Flood
Preparedness Review Meeting by His Excellency Governor of Assam on 28th May, 2025, (ii) Video
Conference with the District Commissioners by Hon’ble Chief Minister on 30th May 2025, (iii) District
level Flood Preparedness review by Hon’ble Minister, Revenue & DM Department, Assam along with
field visit in 6 districts (24th – 26th May, 2025), (iv) State Level Flood Preparedness Review Meeting by
Hon’ble Chief Secretary, Assam on 17th May, 2025, (v) Video conferencing with the DDMAs to review
flood preparedness at the district level conducted on 27th March 2025.
NDRF teams from 1st Bn. and 12th Bn. have been pre-positioned at eight (8) strategic locations of the
state of Assam namely Silchar, Jorhat, Barpeta, Bongaigaon (1 Bn. NDRF), Dibrugarh, Tezpur, Sivasagar
st
and Titabor (12 Bn. NDRF) for effective and prompt response during flood. Besides, five companies of
th
State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) were also deployed in 58 locations of Assam along with rescue
boats and deep divers. Besides, ASDMA also deployed rescue boats, AAPDA Mitra volunteers and DDRF
teams in selected locations in certain vulnerable locations. These proactive preparedness measures lead
to substantive reduction of human lives lost and properties during the flood as compared to the severity
of the flood situation.
Further, ASDMA receives FLEWS (Flood Early Warning System) alerts from North Eastern Space
Application Centre (NESAC) within 12 to 48 hrs lead time in the category of Low, Moderate, High and
Very High alerts and these alerts are disseminated to DDMAs, Revenue Circle Offices, concerned
authorities of the Govt. of Assam and other response agencies.

2.5 REASONS FOR THE ASSAM FLOODS 2025:
 The State has a large network of rivers & tributaries originating from the Upper catchments with high
gradient.
 Assam faced 1st wave of flood occurred due to heavy to very heavy rainfall in Assam and in the
neighboring States.
 Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya Mizoram, Nagaland and Tripura recorded an excess
rainfall with 195%, 158%, 403%, 279%, 313%, 316%, 112% deviation from the normal from 28th - 31st
May, 2025 affecting a population of 6.79 lakhs on 4th June, 2025 in 21 districts.
 Eventually situation started improving after 5th June, 2025.
 Moreover, incessant rainfall in Bhutan as well as the release of water from Khangdong (Kopili, Dima
Hasao) Panyor (Arunachal Pradesh) and Doyang Hydel Power Project (Nagaland) dams are other
important causes for floods in downstream districts i.e. Barpeta, Hojai, Nagaon, Lakhimpur and
Golaghat districts.

District Commissioners of all DDMAs of Assam. Hon’ble Chief Minister instructed all the District
Commissioners to establish effective coordination with NDRF and SDRF teams, to ensure a prompt response

(DDMAs) and concerned line departments of the State Government, total requirement of funds covered
under SDRF/NDRF for (i) rescue & relief operation (₹62.98 crores), (ii) Sectoral damages other than core

is amounting to ₹ 2871.21 Cr. (in words Two Thousand Eight hundred Seventy One Crore and Twenty one
Lakhs only)
Government of India is therefore, requested to provide financial assistance and help the State to recover
from the severe damages caused by the multiple waves of floods in 2025.
